1. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

1.1 Objective¶

The goal of this analysis is to explore the ICBC crash dataset (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tcashion/icbc-vehicle-crash-dataset/data), understand its structure and quality, identify patterns related to casualty crashes, and determine whether the available variables are suitable for predicting high-risk intersections.

This EDA will:

  • Examine data quality and completeness
  • Understand the distribution of casualty crashes
  • Explore temporal and geographic patterns
  • Investigate relationships between crash characteristics and crash severity
  • Generate observations that guide feature engineering and model selection

Intersection data QA¶

In [8]:
# handle intersection names 
def normalize_intersection(row):
    street1 = str(row["Street Full Name (ifnull)"]).strip().upper()
    street2 = str(row["Cross Street Full Name"]).strip().upper()

    streets = sorted([street1, street2])

    return " @ ".join(streets)

In [12]:
original_intersections = (
    intersection_df["Street Full Name (ifnull)"].str.strip().str.upper()
    + " @ "
    + intersection_df["Cross Street Full Name"].str.strip().str.upper()
)

print("Original unique intersection IDs:", original_intersections.nunique())
print("Normalized unique intersections:", intersection_df["Intersection"].nunique())
print(
    "Duplicate directional IDs consolidated:",
    original_intersections.nunique() - intersection_df["Intersection"].nunique(),
)

Original unique intersection IDs: 9363
Normalized unique intersections: 5617
Duplicate directional IDs consolidated: 3746

Intersection identifiers were constructed from the two street names and normalized by alphabetically sorting the street pair. This prevents the same physical intersection from being treated as separate locations when the street order is reversed (e.g., BOUNDARY RD @ GRANDVIEW HWY and GRANDVIEW HWY @ BOUNDARY RD). Normalization reduced the number of unique intersection identifiers from 9,363 to 5,617, consolidating 3,746 duplicate directional identifiers.

In [36]:
corr = summary["Total_Crashes"].corr(summary["Casualty_Crashes"])
print(f"Pearson correlation: {corr:.3f}")

Pearson correlation: 0.960
  • There is a strong positive relationship between the total number of crashes at an intersection and the number of casualty crashes. Intersections with higher crash volumes also tend to experience more injury crashes.
  • Most intersections cluster near the origin, indicating that the majority of Vancouver intersections experience relatively few crashes over the five-year period.
  • A small number of intersections stand out as high-volume outliers, with Boundary Rd @ Grandview Hwy being the most prominent.
  • There are a few intersections with similar total crash counts but noticeably different casualty counts (for example, W 41st Ave @ Cambie St versus Kingsway @ Victoria Dr), suggesting that crash volume alone may not fully explain casualty risk.

Within the Vancouver subset, approximately 10.2% of records are missing latitude and longitude coordinates. These fields are always missing together, indicating a common source of missingness rather than independent data quality issues. Since the majority (89.8%) of crash records retain valid coordinates, there is sufficient spatial information for exploratory geographic analyses. Coordinate availability will be considered when selecting records for any map-based visualizations.

1.2 Summary of Findings¶

The EDA focused on Vancouver crashes from 2018–2022. I looked at data quality, crash severity, temporal patterns, crash characteristics, and differences between intersections.

Key Findings¶

  • The Vancouver subset contains approximately 225,000 crash records between 2018 - 2022, with roughly 20% classified as casualty crashes and 80% as property-damage-only crashes. This represents a moderately imbalanced classification problem.

  • Crash frequency varies over time. Most crashes occur during weekday daytime and afternoon hours (approximately 12:00–18:00), with fewer crashes overnight. A noticeable decline in crash counts is observed during 2020, followed by recovery in 2021–2022.

  • Rear-end, side-impact, and single-vehicle collisions are the most common crash configurations within Vancouver.

  • Several binary crash characteristics show meaningful relationships with casualty crashes. Crashes involving pedestrians, cyclists, motorcycles, and intersections are substantially more likely to result in injuries than the overall average, while parking lot crashes are rarely casualty crashes.

  • A relatively small number of intersections account for a disproportionately large number of crashes, suggesting that historical intersection crash patterns may be valuable predictors of future casualty risk.

  • Missing data is generally limited. The primary missing field is Cross Street Full Name, which is expected because many crashes occur away from intersections. This will be considered during feature engineering.

Implications for Modeling¶

The exploratory analysis suggests that historical crash records contain meaningful information for predicting future casualty crash risk at Vancouver intersections. Variables describing crash history, temporal patterns, crash configuration, and vulnerable road user involvement exhibit meaningful associations with casualty crashes and will be explored as candidate predictive features during model development.

The client's objective is interpreted as forecasting future casualty crash risk to prioritize engineering interventions. Because the dataset ends in 2022, no 2023 observations are available for evaluating a true forward prediction. Therefore, this project uses historical crash information available through 2021 to predict casualty crashes in 2022. This creates a realistic historical forecasting scenario that allows model performance to be quantitatively evaluated. Once validated, the same modeling approach could be retrained using all available data and applied operationally to forecast risk in subsequent years.

The next phase of the project will aggregate individual crash records into intersection-year summaries and engineer historical features for each intersection.

2. Predictive Modeling¶

Modeling Strategy¶

The objective of the modeling phase is to identify Vancouver intersections that are most likely to experience casualty crashes in the future so that Engineering Services can prioritize locations for safety review.

The available dataset contains crash records from 2018–2022. To evaluate the forecasting approach using observed data, crashes from 2018–2021 will be used to construct historical features for each intersection, while the number of casualty crashes occurring in 2022 will be used as the prediction target.

Each row in the modeling dataset therefore represents a Vancouver intersection rather than an individual crash.

The primary prediction target is:

2022 casualty crash count per intersection

Historical features will summarize each intersection's previous crash activity, including total crash volume, casualty crash history, crash characteristics, vulnerable road user involvement, and temporal patterns.

Model performance will be evaluated both by its ability to predict casualty crash counts and, more importantly for the client, by how effectively it identifies the highest-risk intersections. Particular attention will therefore be given to the model's top-30 ranked intersections.

There are 8,755 intersections, but 6,243 (71.3%) had zero casualty crashes in 2022. The mean is only 0.78 while the maximum is 34, so the target is extremely right-skewed and zero-heavy.

The client mainly cares about whether our model gets the highest-risk ~30 intersections right, not whether it predicts every low-risk intersection perfectly.

So the eventual comparisons could be:

  • Baseline: rank by historical crash count alone.
  • Random Forest / Gradient Boosting: captures nonlinear relationships between historical characteristics and future casualty counts.

# overlap of top-30 intersections by casualty crashes in 2021 and 2022
actual_top30 = set(
    model_data.nlargest(30, "Target_Casualty_Crashes_2022")["Intersection"]
)

# nlargest returns a DataFrame, so we need to select the "Intersection" column and convert it to a set for comparison
baseline_top30 = set(model_data.nlargest(30, "Casualty_Crashes_2021")["Intersection"])

baseline_overlap = len(actual_top30 & baseline_top30)

print(f"Baseline Top-30 overlap:{baseline_overlap}/30")

Baseline Top-30 overlap:16/30

Note: nlargest arbitrarily takes the top 30.

A simple historical baseline was established by assuming that each intersection's casualty crash count in 2022 would equal its casualty crash count in 2021.

The baseline achieved:

  • MAE: 0.624 casualty crashes
  • RMSE: 1.366 casualty crashes
  • Top-30 overlap: 14/30 intersections (46.7%)

Although the average prediction error is relatively small, this partly reflects the large number of intersections with few or no casualty crashes. More importantly for the stakeholder, using the previous year's casualty count alone identifies fewer than half of the 30 highest-casualty intersections in 2022.

The predictive models will therefore be evaluated not only on overall prediction error, but also on whether they improve identification of the highest-risk intersections relative to this historical baseline.

2.5 Historical forecasting samples¶

In [64]:
def build_forecast_dataset(df, target_year):
    history = df[df["Date Of Loss Year"] < target_year].copy()
    future = df[df["Date Of Loss Year"] == target_year].copy()

    # binary indicators
    history["Casualty"] = (
        history["Crash Severity"] == "CASUALTY CRASH"
    ).astype(int)

    history["Pedestrian"] = (
        history["Pedestrian Involved"] == "Yes"
    ).astype(int)

    history["Cyclist"] = (
        history["Cyclist Involved"] == "Yes"
    ).astype(int)

    history["Motorcycle"] = (
        history["Motorcycle Involved"] == "Yes"
    ).astype(int)

    history["Heavy_Vehicle"] = (
        history["Heavy Veh Involved"] == "Yes"
    ).astype(int)

    history["Parked_Vehicle"] = (
        history["Parked Vehicle Involved"] == "Yes"
    ).astype(int)

    # cumulative historical features
    features = history.groupby("Intersection").agg(
        Total_Crashes=("Intersection", "size"),
        Historical_Casualty_Crashes=("Casualty", "sum"),
        Pedestrian_Crashes=("Pedestrian", "sum"),
        Cyclist_Crashes=("Cyclist", "sum"),
        Motorcycle_Crashes=("Motorcycle", "sum"),
        Heavy_Vehicle_Crashes=("Heavy_Vehicle", "sum"),
        Parked_Vehicle_Crashes=("Parked_Vehicle", "sum"),
    ).reset_index()

    features["Historical_Casualty_Rate"] = (
        features["Historical_Casualty_Crashes"]
        / features["Total_Crashes"]
    )

    # temporal features: previous year and two years ago crash counts and casualty counts
    previous_year = target_year - 1
    two_years_ago = target_year - 2

    def get_year_counts(year):
        year_df = history[
            history["Date Of Loss Year"] == year
        ]

        crashes = year_df.groupby("Intersection").size()

        casualties = (
            year_df[
                year_df["Crash Severity"] == "CASUALTY CRASH"
            ]
            .groupby("Intersection")
            .size()
        )

        return crashes, casualties

    prev_crashes, prev_casualties = get_year_counts(previous_year)
    older_crashes, older_casualties = get_year_counts(two_years_ago)

    features["Previous_Year_Crashes"] = (
        features["Intersection"].map(prev_crashes).fillna(0)
    )

    features["Previous_Year_Casualty_Crashes"] = (
        features["Intersection"].map(prev_casualties).fillna(0)
    )

    features["Two_Years_Ago_Crashes"] = (
        features["Intersection"].map(older_crashes).fillna(0)
    )

    features["Two_Years_Ago_Casualty_Crashes"] = (
        features["Intersection"].map(older_casualties).fillna(0)
    )

    # casualty rate in most recent year
    features["Previous_Year_Casualty_Rate"] = np.where(
        features["Previous_Year_Crashes"] > 0,
        features["Previous_Year_Casualty_Crashes"]
        / features["Previous_Year_Crashes"],
        0
    )

    # average of previous two years
    features["Two_Year_Avg_Crashes"] = (
        features["Previous_Year_Crashes"]
        + features["Two_Years_Ago_Crashes"]
    ) / 2

    features["Two_Year_Avg_Casualties"] = (
        features["Previous_Year_Casualty_Crashes"]
        + features["Two_Years_Ago_Casualty_Crashes"]
    ) / 2

    # change from two years ago to previous year
    features["Crash_Trend"] = (
        features["Previous_Year_Crashes"]
        - features["Two_Years_Ago_Crashes"]
    )

    features["Casualty_Trend"] = (
        features["Previous_Year_Casualty_Crashes"]
        - features["Two_Years_Ago_Casualty_Crashes"]
    )


    target = (
        future[
            future["Crash Severity"] == "CASUALTY CRASH"
        ]
        .groupby("Intersection")
        .size()
        .rename("Target")
    )

    features = features.merge(
        target,
        on="Intersection",
        how="left"
    )

    features["Target"] = features["Target"].fillna(0)
    features["Target_Year"] = target_year

    return features

2.6 Random Forest¶

2.6.1 Random Forest Regressor - Cumulative Historical Features¶

    "Total_Crashes",
    "Historical_Casualty_Crashes",
    "Historical_Casualty_Rate",
    "Pedestrian_Crashes",
    "Cyclist_Crashes",
    "Motorcycle_Crashes",
    "Heavy_Vehicle_Crashes",
    "Parked_Vehicle_Crashes",
    "Previous_Year_Crashes",
    "Previous_Year_Casualty_Crashes",

    # temporal features
    "Two_Years_Ago_Crashes",

    "Previous_Year_Casualty_Rate",
    "Two_Year_Avg_Crashes",
    "Two_Year_Avg_Casualties",
    "Crash_Trend",
    "Casualty_Trend",
]

X_train = training_data[feature_cols]
y_train = training_data["Target"]

X_test = test_data[feature_cols]
y_test = test_data["Target"]

# train a random forest regressor
rf = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=300, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1, min_samples_leaf=2
)

rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

rf_pred = rf.predict(X_test)

# evaluate the model
rf_mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, rf_pred)
rf_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, rf_pred))

print(f"Random Forest MAE:  {rf_mae:.3f}")
print(f"Random Forest RMSE: {rf_rmse:.3f}")

Looking at the recalls above, the RF is much better at identifying the general high-risk pool rather than the 17/30 initially suggested.

Most of the actual high-risk intersections aren't being ranked hundreds or thousands of places away. The model struggles with precise ordering near the top.

BOUNDARY RD @ MARINE WAY is actual rank 3 but predicted 53, E BROADWAY @ RUPERT ST is actual rank 14 but predicted 74, and GRANVILLE ST @ W 57TH AVE is actual rank 28 but predicted 86. Those are genuine misses worth understanding. On the other hand, JOYCE ST @ KINGSWAY is actual #2 and predicted #31

Historical_Casualty_Crashes accounts for ~79% of the Random Forest's feature importance. Everything else is dramatically smaller.

The RF has learned that: Intersections that had lots of casualty crashes historically will probably have lots of casualty crashes next year.

This leads me to think that there is a feature design issue. Historical_Casualty_Crashes is a cumulative count (2018 + 2019 + 2020 + 2021)m but when predicting 2020 during training, it's only 2018 + 2019.

Several of the features are also redundant:

  • Historical_Casualty_Crashes
  • Previous_Year_Casualty_Crashes
  • Two_Years_Ago_Casualty_Crashes
  • Two_Year_Avg_Casualties
  • Casualty_Trend

Next steps would be to compare compare cumulative-history features against a fixed recent-history window.

Fixed-Window Feature Experiment results¶

A second Random Forest model was evaluated using only features derived from the previous two years, removing cumulative historical crash measures. This was intended to test whether recent crash patterns provided stronger predictive information than an intersection's full historical record.

The fixed-window model performed worse than the cumulative-history model across MAE, RMSE, Top-30 overlap, and Recall@K. This suggests that longer-term historical crash patterns provide useful predictive information for identifying high-risk intersections. Therefore, the cumulative-history feature set was retained for subsequent modeling.

tuning_results = []

for p in params:
    model = RandomForestRegressor(**p, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)

    model.fit(X_tune_train, y_tune_train)

    pred = model.predict(X_tune_val)

    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_tune_val, pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_tune_val, pred))

    temp = val_2021[["Intersection", "Target"]].copy()
    temp["Predicted"] = pred

    actual_top30 = set(temp.nlargest(30, "Target")["Intersection"])

    predicted_top30 = set(temp.nlargest(30, "Predicted")["Intersection"])

    top30 = len(actual_top30 & predicted_top30)

    tuning_results.append({**p, "MAE": mae, "RMSE": rmse, "Top30": top30})

tuning_results = pd.DataFrame(tuning_results)

display(tuning_results.sort_values(["Top30", "RMSE"], ascending=[False, True]))

Summary¶

Random Forest hyperparameters were selected using the earlier forecasting periods, leaving 2022 as the held-out test year. Top-30 overlap decreased slightly from 17 to 16 intersections, while Recall@50 remained 86.7% and Recall@75 remained 100%.

These results indicate that tuning improved overall casualty-count prediction while maintaining similar high-risk ranking performance. The tuned Random Forest was therefore retained as the final Random Forest specification.

    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_iter=300,
    max_leaf_nodes=31,
    min_samples_leaf=20,
    l2_regularization=1.0,
    random_state=42,
)

gb.fit(X_train, y_train)

gb_pred = gb.predict(X_test)

# casualty crash counts cannot be negative
gb_pred = np.maximum(gb_pred, 0)

gb_mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, gb_pred)
gb_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, gb_pred))

print(f"Gradient Boosting MAE:  {gb_mae:.3f}")
print(f"Gradient Boosting RMSE: {gb_rmse:.3f}")

2.5 Model Selection¶

Random Forest and Gradient Boosting regression were compared against a historical baseline for predicting casualty crashes at Vancouver intersections. Gradient Boosting achieved the highest strict Top-30 overlap, identifying 17 of the actual Top-30 intersections compared with 16 for Random Forest. However, the tuned Random Forest achieved the lowest overall prediction error, with an MAE of 0.775 and RMSE of 1.546 compared with 0.802 and 1.702 for Gradient Boosting.

The tuned Random Forest also retained strong ranking performance beyond the strict Top-30 cutoff, capturing 86.7% of the actual Top-30 intersections within its predicted Top 50 and 100% within its Top 75. Based on its stronger casualty-count accuracy while maintaining comparable high-risk ranking performance, the tuned Random Forest was selected as the final model.

2023 Intersection Risk Forecast¶

The final Random Forest model was retrained using all available historical forecasting data through 2022 and used to estimate casualty crashes at Vancouver intersections for 2023. Intersections were ranked by their predicted casualty crash count, consistent with the client's objective of identifying approximately 30 locations for engineering review.

To assess the stability of the ranking, each of the 500 trees in the Random Forest was also used to independently rank intersections. Top-30 stability represents the percentage of trees in which an intersection appeared among the 30 highest-risk locations.

The highest-ranked locations show strong agreement across the forest. For example, Boundary Rd @ Grandview Hwy was ranked first with approximately 46 predicted casualty crashes and appeared in the Top 30 in 97.8% of trees. The first eight intersections each achieved at minimum 88% Top-30 stability.

Stability decreases further down the ranking, indicating substantially greater uncertainty around the exact composition of the lower portion of the Top 30. Thus, the ranking could more appropriately be interpreted as identifying a high-risk priority group rather than establishing a precise ordering between similarly ranked intersections.

Feature importance was examined to understand which historical crash characteristics contributed most strongly to the Random Forest's predictions. These values describe how useful each feature was to the model across all intersections and should not be interpreted as causal effects.

Historical casualty crash frequency was the strongest predictor of future casualty crashes, indicating that intersections with persistent histories of injury-producing collisions tend to remain high-risk. Total crash volume and recent casualty history also contributed to the predictions, while characteristics such as pedestrian, cyclist, motorcycle, and heavy-vehicle involvement provided additional information about the historical crash profile of each intersection.

Global feature importance explains the model's overall behavior but does not explain why a specific intersection received a high prediction. Intersection-level characteristics are therefore examined

The highest-ranked locations generally have substantial historical crash volumes and casualty crash histories. However, the intersections differ in their recent trends and crash composition.

For example, Boundary Rd @ Grandview Hwy has the highest predicted casualty crash count and also has the largest historical crash volume among the highest-ranked locations. Other locations exhibit different patterns. Kingsway @ Knight St experienced increasing total and casualty crashes in the most recent year, while E 49th Ave @ Knight St experienced a substantial decline in casualty crashes despite remaining highly ranked based on its broader historical record.

These characteristics provide context for the rankings but should not be interpreted as causal explanations. The model's intersection-specific predictions are examined in the following section to identify which features contributed most strongly to individual predictions.

3.3 Top 30 Crash profiles¶

The forecast tells us which intersections are expected to have higher casualty crash risk, but not what might be worth investigating at each location. To add that context, I compared the crash profiles of the predicted Top 30 against Vancouver intersections overall.

What kinds of crashes historically characterize the intersections that the model predicts will be highest-risk in 2023?¶

Crash profiles were constructed using road-user and vehicle involvement, temporal characteristics, and crash configuration. These included pedestrian, cyclist, motorcycle, and heavy-vehicle involvement; morning peak, afternoon peak, nighttime, and weekend crashes; and common crash configurations such as rear-end, side-impact, single-vehicle, head-on, and same-direction sideswipe crashes.

For each characteristic, a relative prevalence index was calculated by dividing its proportion of crashes at an individual intersection by its proportion across all Vancouver intersection crashes. An index of 1.0 therefore represents the Vancouver-wide baseline, while an index of 1.5 indicates that the characteristic is 50% more prevalent at that intersection. Only characteristics with an index of at least 1.25 were highlighted, and a maximum of three characteristics were retained for each intersection.

The results above suggest that predicted high-risk intersections do not share a single crash profile.

E.g. At Boundary Rd @ Grandview Hwy, rear-end crashes are 1.76 times as prevalent as the Vancouver baseline, accompanied by elevated nighttime (1.38×) and heavy-vehicle (1.26×) involvement. Knight St @ SE Marine Dr similarly shows elevated rear-end crashes (1.83×), heavy-vehicle involvement (1.68×), and morning-peak crashes (1.43×). At E 1st Ave @ Hwy 1, rear-end crashes are more than twice as prevalent as the citywide baseline (2.13×).

Main St @ Terminal Ave has pedestrian involvement at 1.86 times the Vancouver baseline, while Clark Dr @ E Broadway has motorcycle involvement at 2.50 times the baseline and heavy-vehicle involvement at 1.63 times the baseline. Boundary Rd @ Marine Way is particularly characterized by heavy-vehicle involvement (2.21×), together with elevated rear-end and morning-peak crashes (both 1.81×). E Hastings St @ Nanaimo St also has elevated heavy-vehicle (2.04×) and pedestrian (1.64×) involvement.

Head-on crashes are disproportionately represented at locations including E 49th Ave @ Victoria Dr (2.28×), Denman St @ W Georgia St (2.05×), and E 33rd Ave @ Knight St (2.04×). Meanwhile, Granville St @ W King Edward Ave shows elevated same-direction sideswipe crashes (1.51×) alongside morning-peak (1.54×) and heavy-vehicle (1.39×) activity.

Some predicted priority intersections have no crash characteristic exceeding the 1.25 threshold (as reflected as Nan). This does not indicate that these locations are low risk; rather, their historical crash composition is relatively similar to the Vancouver-wide distribution despite their high predicted casualty crash counts.

It should be noted that these profiles are descriptive rather than causal.

For example, a higher rate of nighttime crashes does not necessarily mean that poor lighting is causing crashes, but it does suggest that lighting and visibility may be worth investigating. Similarly, higher pedestrian involvement could point engineers toward crossing conditions or turning conflicts, while heavy-vehicle involvement could suggest looking at vehicle movements or intersection geometry. Patterns in rear-end or head-on crashes could also help identify traffic flow or conflict issues. Overall, the forecast ranking helps identify which intersections should be prioritized, while the crash profiles provide additional context on what engineers should look for when reviewing each location.

Splitting the profile into tiers via a priority score¶

Priority Score=0.50(Forecast Risk)+0.30(Stability)+0.20(Crash Profile Strength)

  • 50% Forecast risk - is the main objective of the model
  • 30% Stability - as predictions that consistently remain in the Top 30 should be rewarded
  • 20% Profile strength - reward locations with a particularly overrepresented crash characteristic

The priority scores show a clear separation between the first eight intersections and the rest of the predicted Top 30. Scores remain above 60 through rank 8, before dropping from 60.73 to 41.59 between ranks 8 and 9. Rather than selecting an arbitrary score threshold, this natural break was used to identify the highest-priority group for engineering review.

The priority score's weights are an estimation and simply acts as an suggestion, however the drop in score is indicative of an immediate 'tier' of intersections that should be reviewed.

4. Recommended Engineering Priorities¶

4.1 Summary of findings¶

This analysis used historical Vancouver crash data to identify intersections that may be higher priorities for engineering review. After cleaning and normalizing the intersection data, the Random Forest was selected then fine tuned. The tuned Random Forest performed best overall, with an MAE of 0.775 and RMSE of 1.546, improving on the historical baseline. It identified 16/30 of the actual Top 30 intersections, increasing to 70% recall within the Top 40 and 86.7% within the Top 50.

The final model was then used to predict casualty crashes for 2023. Boundary Rd @ Grandview Hwy was ranked first, with around 46 predicted casualty crashes and 97.8% Top-30 stability. Forecast stability measures how consistently an intersection appears in the predicted Top 30 across repeated model predictions. For each run, the Random Forest was refit/resampled and the percentage of runs where an intersection remained in the Top 30 was recorded. For example, a stability of 97.8% means the intersection appeared in the Top 30 in 97.8% of runs. Higher stability suggests that an intersection's priority ranking is less sensitive to variation in the model.

The predicted Top 30 were then profiled to find crash characteristics that occur more often at each intersection compared relatively to the Vancouver average, with a weighting of 1.25x the vancouver wide average being flagged.

Overall, the results give us two main things: which intersections should be looked at first, and what crash patterns may be worth investigating at each one. The following section uses these results to group intersections into different engineering priority levels.

4.2 Flagged Intersections¶

To combine the results into a final engineering priority ranking, a composite priority score was calculated for each of the predicted Top 30 intersections. The score combines three parts of the analysis: the predicted number of casualty crashes, forecast stability, and the strength of the most overrepresented crash characteristic at the intersection. These represent the overall predicted risk, confidence in the ranking, and whether there is a specific crash pattern that may be useful for engineering review.

Predicted casualty crashes were given the greatest weight because the main goal of the analysis is to identify intersections with the highest expected casualty crash risk. Forecast stability was included to give more weight to intersections that consistently appeared in the Top 30 across repeated model runs, while crash profile strength was included as a smaller component to identify locations with particularly strong crash patterns.

The composite score was calculated as:

Priority Score=0.50(Forecast Risk)+0.30(Forecast Stability)+0.20(Crash Profile Strength)

It should be noted that the score is intended as a prioritization tool rather than a measure of absolute inspection safety. A high score means that an intersection should receive earlier engineering review.

4.3 Conclusion¶

The analysis showed that historical crash data can be used to identify intersections with higher future casualty crash risk. The tuned Random Forest improved on the historical baseline and was used to forecast 2023 casualty crashes, with forecast stability used to measure how consistent these predictions were.

Crash profiles were then used to identify patterns that may help explain what is happening at each intersection, and these results were combined into a final engineering priority score. This identified eight intersections as the strongest candidates for engineering review, providing both a way to prioritize where attention should go first and what crash patterns may be worth investigating.
